title: Newton's Laws of Motion
tagline: Inertia, Newton's three laws, momentum and impulse, conservation of linear momentum, equilibrium of concurrent forces, and friction.

Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Physics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Newton's laws of motion are the foundation of classical mechanics. They tell us how forces change motion and how motion is described in terms of mass and momentum. This chapter begins with the idea of inertia, then states and applies each of Newton's three laws. We look at momentum and impulse, use the idea of conservation of linear momentum in problems where external forces are balanced or absent, and finish with the everyday but subtle topic of friction, including the difference between static and kinetic friction.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Inertia; Newton's three laws; momentum and impulse; conservation of linear momentum; equilibrium of concurrent forces; static and kinetic friction; rolling friction; lubrication

learningOutcomes: State Newton's three laws of motion and identify what each one describes.
Use F = ma in simple problems.
Define momentum and use the impulse-momentum idea.
Apply conservation of linear momentum to suitable simple cases.
Distinguish static friction from kinetic friction.
Draw a clear free-body diagram before applying the laws.

blocks.text: The first law says that a body remains at rest, or moves with constant velocity, unless a net external force acts on it. This tendency to resist changes in motion is called inertia. The first law is not just a special case of the second; it defines the idea of an inertial frame of reference, in which the law holds. A simple everyday example is that a book on a table stays still until something pushes or pulls it, and a moving object would keep moving forever if friction and other forces did not slow it down.

items: The first law describes the zero-net-force case.
Inertia is the resistance to change in motion.
The law defines inertial frames.
A body does not need a force to keep moving at constant velocity.

items.text: When a bus stops suddenly, passengers tend to keep moving forward because of inertia. The body continues in its state of motion unless a force acts.
items.note: The first law reminds us that motion does not need a continuous push to persist.

blocks.text: The second law relates force, mass and acceleration. For a constant mass, the net force on a body equals mass times acceleration. The more general statement is that the rate of change of momentum equals the net external force. This means a small force acting for a long time can produce the same change in momentum as a large force acting briefly, provided the impulse is the same.

items: Net force = mass x acceleration for constant mass.
More generally, net force = rate of change of momentum.
The direction of acceleration is the direction of the net force.
The law is about net force, not a single individual force.

items.text: If two equal forces pull in opposite directions on a box, the net force is zero and the acceleration is zero, even though the individual forces are not zero.
items.note: The second law uses the vector sum of forces, not any one force in isolation.

blocks.text: The third law says that whenever one body exerts a force on another, the second body exerts an equal and opposite force on the first. These forces are often called action and reaction, but they are not a cause-and-effect sequence in time; they occur together. A very important point is that the two forces act on different bodies, so they do not cancel on a single free-body diagram.

items: Action and reaction are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
They act on different bodies.
They do not cancel each other on one body's free-body diagram.
They are simultaneous, not one happening after the other.

items.text: When a swimmer pushes water backward, the water pushes the swimmer forward. The two forces are equal and opposite, but each acts on a different object.
items.note: If both forces acted on the swimmer, motion would never start; the third-law pair explains why motion is possible.

blocks.text: Momentum is mass times velocity, and it is a vector. Impulse is the change in momentum caused by a force acting over a time interval. For a constant force, impulse equals force times time. For a varying force, impulse is the area under the force-time graph. The impulse-momentum idea is especially useful when the force changes with time, such as in a collision.

items: Momentum = mass x velocity.
Impulse = change in momentum.
For constant force, impulse = force x time.
For varying force, impulse is the area under the force-time curve.

items.text: A fielder lowering the hands while catching a ball increases the time of the catch, which reduces the average force on the hands for the same change in momentum.
items.note: The same momentum change can be achieved with a smaller force if the time is longer.

blocks.text: If no external force acts on a system, its total linear momentum stays constant. This is conservation of linear momentum. It is useful in problems involving collisions, explosions, recoil and similar situations, because it can give the result without knowing the detailed forces during the event. The law applies to the whole system, not necessarily to each part of it.

items: Total momentum is conserved when net external force is zero.
Momentum is a vector, so direction matters.
The law is powerful when internal forces are complicated.
It applies to systems, not always to individual parts.

items.text: When two ice skaters push each other apart, their total momentum before and after is the same, provided friction is small enough to ignore.
items.note: Each skater's momentum changes, but the sum of the two momenta stays constant.

blocks.text: A body is in equilibrium when the net force on it is zero. For several forces meeting at a point, this means the vector sum of the forces is zero. Friction is a force that opposes relative motion between surfaces. Static friction acts when surfaces are not slipping relative to each other, and its value adjusts up to a limiting maximum. Kinetic friction acts when surfaces are sliding. Lubrication reduces friction by keeping the surfaces apart.

items: Equilibrium means zero net force.
Static friction adjusts to the needed value, up to a maximum.
Kinetic friction acts when surfaces slide.
Rough surfaces produce more friction than smooth ones, in general.
Lubrication reduces friction by preventing direct contact.

items.text: If a box is pushed with a small force and does not move, static friction equals the push. As the push increases, static friction increases until it reaches its maximum, after which the box slides.
items.note: Static friction is not always equal to its maximum; it is only the value needed to prevent motion up to that limit.

keyPoints: The first law defines inertia and inertial frames.
The second law relates net force, mass and acceleration, or rate of change of momentum.
The third law forces are equal, opposite and act on different bodies.
Momentum is conserved when net external force is zero.
Static friction adjusts up to a maximum; kinetic friction acts during sliding.
Always draw a free-body diagram before applying the laws.
examFocus: When using F = ma, remember it is the net force on the body that matters, not one force alone.
Do not cancel action and reaction forces on the same object; they act on different bodies.

vocabulary.meaning: The tendency of a body to resist changes in its state of motion.
The product of mass and velocity; a vector quantity.
The change in momentum produced by a force over a time interval.
A state in which the net force on a body is zero.
The friction force that prevents relative motion between surfaces at rest.
The friction force between surfaces that are sliding relative to each other.

questions.explanation: The first law describes inertia, the tendency to resist changes in motion.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing inertia with force or energy.

questions.prompt: Action and reaction forces act on:
questions.explanation: The third-law pair acts on different bodies, so they do not cancel on one body.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking they act on the same object and therefore cancel.

questions.answer: Impulse equals the change in momentum. For a constant force, impulse = force x time = change in momentum.
questions.explanation: Impulse and momentum change are equivalent ideas.
questions.commonMistake: Saying impulse is the force itself, rather than the force multiplied by time.

questions.prompt: Why does a fielder lower the hands while catching a fast ball?
questions.answer: Lowering the hands increases the time of the catch, which reduces the average force for the same change in momentum.
questions.explanation: This is an application of the impulse-momentum idea.
questions.commonMistake: Saying it is only to avoid pain, without mentioning time and force.

questions.prompt: A 5 kg box is pulled with a horizontal force of 20 N on a rough surface, and the box moves at constant velocity. Find the friction force.
questions.answer: Since velocity is constant, net force is zero, so friction force = 20 N opposite to the pull.
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the applied force and friction must balance.
questions.commonMistake: Setting friction equal to mu N without checking that the box is not accelerating.
